lessons.title: Getting Started
lessons.summary: Setting up Python and running your first script.
lessons.body:
Python is an interpreted language, which means you write code in a plain text file and the Python interpreter reads and runs it line by line — no separate compile step. On Linux Mint, Python 3 is already installed; you just need an editor (even a simple one like Geany or VS Code works fine) and a terminal.

A Python file ends in .py. The simplest possible program is one line:

 print("Hello, sendero!")

Save that as hello.py and run it from a terminal with `python3 hello.py`. The print() function is your window into what a program is doing — you'll use it constantly, especially while learning.

Python also has an interactive mode: type `python3` alone in a terminal and you get a prompt (>>>) where you can type one line at a time and see results immediately. It's a great scratchpad for testing small ideas before putting them in a real script.

One habit worth building early: read error messages instead of skimming past them. Python's errors (called "tracebacks") point to the exact line and describe what went wrong — they're one of the most beginner-friendly error systems in any language.

— Based on: Python Crash Course ch.1, Automate the Boring Stuff ch.1 (setup)

lessons.title: Variables and Simple Data Types
lessons.summary: Naming values, strings, numbers, and the philosophy behind readable code.
lessons.body:
A variable is a name attached to a value. Python doesn't require you to declare a variable's type ahead of time — you just assign it:

 name = "Alex"
 age = 34
 height = 5.9

Variable names should be lowercase with underscores (snake_case) and descriptive: `user_age` beats `x`. This isn't just style — code is read far more often than it's written, and a good name saves the next reader (often you, in six months) real time.

Strings are sequences of characters wrapped in quotes. Python gives you a rich set of string methods: `.upper()`, `.lower()`, `.strip()` (removes whitespace from the ends), and f-strings for embedding variables directly in text:

 print(f"{name} is {age} years old.")

Numbers come in two everyday flavors: `int` (whole numbers) and `float` (decimals). Python handles the arithmetic operators you'd expect (+, -, *, /), plus // for integer division and ** for exponents.

Finally, comments (lines starting with #) let you leave notes for humans that Python ignores entirely. Use them to explain *why* code does something, not what it does — the code itself already says what.

— Based on: Python Crash Course ch.2, Automate the Boring Stuff ch.1

lessons.title: Introducing Lists
lessons.summary: Storing and manipulating ordered collections of items.
lessons.body:
A list is an ordered collection, written with square brackets:

 trail_stops = ["camp", "ridge", "summit"]

Items are indexed starting at 0, so `trail_stops[0]` is "camp" and `trail_stops[-1]` (negative indices count from the end) is "summit". You can change an item by assigning to its index: `trail_stops[1] = "overlook"`.

Lists grow and shrink with a handful of methods: `.append(x)` adds to the end, `.insert(i, x)` adds at a position, `.remove(x)` deletes the first matching value, and `.pop()` removes and returns the last item (or a specific index if you pass one).

You can sort a list permanently with `.sort()`, or get a sorted copy without changing the original using `sorted(trail_stops)`. `.reverse()` flips the order in place.

One subtlety worth internalizing early: a list is *mutable* — changing it in one place changes it everywhere it's referenced. This matters once you start passing lists into functions, which comes up soon.

— Based on: Python Crash Course ch.3

lessons.title: Working with Lists
lessons.summary: Looping, ranges, comprehensions, and slicing.
lessons.body:
Looping over a list is one of the most common things you'll do:

 for stop in trail_stops:
 print(f"Next: {stop}")

The `range()` function generates a sequence of numbers, useful for looping a fixed number of times: `for i in range(5):` runs the loop with i = 0,1,2,3,4.

List comprehensions let you build a new list from an existing one in a single, readable line:

 squares = [n**2 for n in range(1, 6)] # [1, 4, 9, 16, 25]

This is one of Python's signature features — once it clicks, you'll reach for it constantly instead of writing a manual loop with .append() calls.

Slicing lets you grab a sub-section of a list: `trail_stops[1:3]` returns items at index 1 and 2 (the end index is exclusive). `trail_stops[:2]` means "from the start," and `trail_stops[1:]` means "to the end."

Tuples are like lists but immutable — once created, they can't be changed. Use them for values that should stay fixed, like coordinates: `location = (18.47, -66.11)`.

— Based on: Python Crash Course ch.4

lessons.title: if Statements and Flow Control
lessons.summary: Branching logic, boolean tests, and while loops.
lessons.body:
An if statement lets a program make decisions:

 if elevation > 3000:
 print("Bring a jacket.")
 elif elevation > 1000:
 print("Layer up.")
 else:
 print("T-shirt weather.")

Conditional tests rely on comparison operators (==, !=, <, >, <=, >=) and can be combined with `and`, `or`, and `not`. Checking membership is common too: `if "camp" in trail_stops:`.

A while loop keeps running as long as a condition stays true — useful when you don't know ahead of time how many iterations you'll need:

 steps = 0
 while steps < 10000:
 steps += walk()

Inside a loop, `break` exits immediately, and `continue` skips to the next iteration without finishing the current one. A common pattern is an input loop that runs until the user types a quit command — you'll build exactly that in the next lesson.

Getting comfortable reading `if`/`elif`/`else` chains and `while` loops is the last piece needed before functions and dictionaries start feeling natural, since almost every real program is built from these same handful of control-flow shapes combined in different orders.

— Based on: Python Crash Course ch.5, Automate the Boring Stuff ch.2

lessons.title: Dictionaries
lessons.summary: Key-value pairs for modeling structured information.
lessons.body:
A dictionary stores key-value pairs — think of it as a lookup table:

 hiker = {"name": "Alex", "pace": "moderate", "trail": "El Yunque"}

You access a value by its key: `hiker["name"]`. Adding or changing an entry is just an assignment: `hiker["pace"] = "fast"`.

Looping through a dictionary is common, and Python gives you a few angles on it:

 for key, value in hiker.items():
 print(f"{key}: {value}")

Use `.keys()` or `.values()` alone if you only need one side. `.get("name", "unknown")` is a safe way to look up a key that might not exist, returning a default instead of raising an error.

Dictionaries nest naturally — a list of dictionaries is the most common shape for real data (think: a list of trail-stop records, each with its own name, elevation, and notes), and a dictionary can hold a list as one of its values just as easily. Once you're comfortable nesting these two structures inside each other, you can model almost any real-world data shape Python will hand you — which is exactly what you'll be doing constantly once you start working with files, CSVs, and APIs later on.

— Based on: Python Crash Course ch.6

lessons.title: User Input and while Loops
lessons.summary: Building interactive programs that respond to the user.
lessons.body:
The `input()` function pauses a program and waits for the user to type something, returning it as a string:

 name = input("What's your name? ")

Combined with a while loop, this is how you build simple interactive programs — quizzes, menus, small games:

 active = True
 while active:
 answer = input("Type 'quit' to stop: ")
 if answer == "quit":
 active = False

A variable like `active` that controls whether a loop keeps running is often called a "flag." Flags make loop logic easier to read than piling multiple conditions into the while line itself.

Note that `input()` always returns a string, even if the user types a number — so `int(input("Age: "))` is a common pattern when you need to do arithmetic on what someone typed.

This pattern — loop, get input, check for a quit condition, act on the input — is the skeleton behind a huge number of small interactive tools, from a number-guessing game to a command-line quiz app.

— Based on: Python Crash Course ch.7

lessons.title: Functions
lessons.summary: Packaging logic into reusable, well-named blocks — and Python's take on first-class functions.
lessons.body:
A function bundles a block of code under a name, so you can run it repeatedly without repeating yourself:

 def greet(name, greeting="Hello"):
 return f"{greeting}, {name}!"

Parameters can have default values (like `greeting` above), which makes them optional when calling the function. `return` sends a value back to whoever called the function; a function with no `return` implicitly returns `None`.

Passing a list or dictionary into a function passes a reference to the same object — changes made inside the function are visible outside it too, since lists and dicts are mutable. This trips up a lot of newcomers, so it's worth testing deliberately once to see it happen.

Python treats functions as first-class objects — meaning a function can be stored in a variable, passed as an argument to another function, or returned from one, exactly like a number or a string:

 def shout(text):
 return text.upper()

 action = shout
 print(action("hello")) # HELLO

A lambda is a small, unnamed function for one-off use, most often as an argument to something like `sorted()`: `sorted(names, key=lambda n: len(n))` sorts by name length. Once functions feel first-class rather than special, decorators and higher-order functions (coming up soon) stop feeling like magic.

— Based on: Python Crash Course ch.8, Python Tricks 3.1–3.2

lessons.title: Writing Cleaner Python
lessons.summary: Idioms that separate working code from Pythonic code.
lessons.body:
Once the basics are solid, a few habits make code noticeably more professional.

Assertions (`assert` statements) are sanity checks you leave in code to catch bugs early: `assert age >= 0, "age can't be negative"`. They're meant for catching your own programming mistakes during development, not for validating user input in a finished program.

The `with` statement (a "context manager") handles setup and cleanup automatically — most famously for files:

 with open("notes.txt") as f:
 text = f.read()

The file is closed automatically when the block ends, even if an error happens inside it. This is safer than manually calling `.close()` and forgetting it under an exception.

Double-underscore ("dunder") methods like `__init__` and `__repr__` are how Python objects hook into built-in behavior — you'll meet more of these in the Classes lessons ahead. A single leading underscore (`_internal`) is a convention signaling "internal use, not part of the public interface," even though Python doesn't enforce it.

For combining variables into text, f-strings (`f"{name} is here"`) are the modern, readable choice — clearer than older `%` formatting or `.format()` calls, and worth defaulting to from here on.

— Based on: Python Tricks 2.1–2.6

lessons.title: Classes
lessons.summary: Modeling real-world things as objects with attributes and behavior.

lessons.title: Classes and OOP, the Pythonic Way
lessons.summary: The small conventions that make custom classes feel native to Python.
lessons.body:
A handful of conventions separate a class that merely works from one that feels native to Python.

Every class benefits from a `__repr__` method — it controls what you see when you print an object or inspect it in a REPL, and a good one shows exactly how to recreate the object:

 def __repr__(self):
 return f"Trail({self.name!r}, {self.distance_km})"

Without it, printing an object gives an unhelpful memory address instead.

Use `is` only to check identity ("is this the exact same object in memory," most often used for `is None`), and `==` to check equality of value — mixing the two up is a common source of subtle bugs.

Custom exception classes let you signal specific problems in your own domain rather than relying on generic ones:

 class TrailClosedError(Exception):
 pass

`namedtuple` (from the `collections` module) gives you lightweight, immutable records with named fields — a nice middle ground between a plain tuple and a full class, when all you need is to bundle a few related values together.

Finally, know the difference between a class variable (shared across every instance) and an instance variable (unique per object) — accidentally treating a mutable class variable (like a list) as if it were per-instance is one of the most common real bugs in beginner object-oriented code.

— Based on: Python Tricks 4.1–4.8

lessons.title: Common Data Structures
lessons.summary: Picking the right container for the job, beyond lists and dicts.
lessons.body:
Python's built-in list and dict cover most needs, but a few specialized structures (mostly from the `collections` module) solve specific problems more cleanly.

A `set` stores unique, unordered values and is ideal for membership tests and de-duplication:

 visited = {"camp", "ridge"}
 visited.add("summit")
 "camp" in visited # fast lookup, and no duplicates possible

A `Counter` (from `collections`) tallies items automatically — handy for counting word frequency or how many times each trail was hiked.

A `deque` (double-ended queue) supports fast additions and removals from *both* ends, unlike a plain list, which is slow to modify at the front. Deques are the natural choice for a queue (first-in-first-out, like people waiting at a trailhead) or a stack (last-in-first-out, like undo history) when performance matters.

For priority-based processing — always handling the most urgent item next — the `heapq` module gives you a priority queue: push items with a priority value, and popping always returns the lowest one first.

The underlying skill here isn't memorizing every structure — it's asking "what operation will I do most often with this data?" before reaching for the default list or dict out of habit.

— Based on: Python Tricks 5.1–5.7

lessons.title: Effective Functions
lessons.summary: Decorators, flexible arguments, and unpacking.
lessons.body:
A decorator wraps a function to add behavior without changing its code — one of Python's more distinctive features:

 def timer(func):
 def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
 import time
 start = time.time()
 result = func(*args, **kwargs)
 print(f"{func.__name__} took {time.time() - start:.3f}s")
 return result
 return wrapper

 @timer
 def slow_task():
 ...

`*args` collects any number of positional arguments into a tuple, and `**kwargs` collects keyword arguments into a dictionary — both let a function accept a flexible number of inputs without you having to predict them all in advance.

Unpacking works in reverse too: `print(*[1, 2, 3])` spreads a list out into separate positional arguments, and `**a_dict` spreads a dictionary out into keyword arguments when calling a function.

Not every function needs to return something — one that just performs an action (printing, saving, sending) and returns nothing (`None` implicitly) is completely normal; forcing a return value where there's no natural one to give just adds noise.

— Based on: Python Tricks 3.3–3.6

lessons.title: Files and Exceptions
lessons.summary: Reading and writing files safely, and handling errors gracefully.
lessons.body:
Working with files follows a predictable shape:

 with open("log.txt", "r") as f:
 contents = f.read()

 with open("log.txt", "a") as f:
 f.write("New entry\n")

The mode string controls behavior: "r" reads, "w" writes (overwriting anything already there), "a" appends. File paths can be relative (to wherever the script is run from) or absolute — Python's `os.path` module has helpers for building paths safely across operating systems.

Things go wrong — files go missing, data is malformed. `try`/`except` catches errors instead of letting the whole program crash:

 try:
 with open("missing.txt") as f:
 data = f.read()
 except FileNotFoundError:
 print("File not found — starting fresh.")

Catch specific exception types rather than a bare `except:`, so you don't accidentally swallow bugs you actually wanted to see. An optional `else` block runs only if no exception occurred, and `finally` always runs, error or not — handy for cleanup.

For structured data, `json.dump()` and `json.load()` write and read Python dictionaries/lists as JSON files directly — this is how the lesson data behind this very app is stored.

— Based on: Python Crash Course ch.10, Automate the Boring Stuff ch.8

lessons.title: Testing Your Code
lessons.summary: Proving your functions actually work, and keeping them working.

lessons.title: Debugging Like a Pro
lessons.summary: Moving beyond print() statements to find bugs faster.
lessons.body:
Every programmer's first debugging tool is `print()`, and it's genuinely fine for quick checks. But it doesn't scale — you end up littering code with prints and manually removing them later.

The `logging` module is the grown-up version: it has severity levels (DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR, CRITICAL), can be turned on or off without deleting code, and can write to a file instead of the terminal:

 import logging
 logging.basicConfig(level=logging.DEBUG, format="%(asctime)s - %(levelname)s - %(message)s")
 logging.debug("Starting trail calculation")

Raising your own exceptions deliberately (`raise ValueError("elevation can't be negative")`) is often clearer than letting a program fail mysteriously three functions later because of bad input it silently accepted.

`assert` statements are a lightweight way to state "this should always be true at this point" — useful while developing, though they can be globally disabled in optimized mode, so never rely on them for real input validation in finished code.

For a stubborn bug, a step debugger (built into most editors, and available in IDLE) lets you pause execution and inspect variables at the exact moment something goes wrong — far faster than guessing where to place the next print statement.

— Based on: Automate the Boring Stuff ch.10

lessons.title: Looping and Iteration, the Pythonic Way
lessons.summary: enumerate, generators, and writing loops that read cleanly.
lessons.body:
A few small habits separate a beginner's loop from an idiomatic one.

Need both the index and the value? Reach for `enumerate()` instead of manually tracking a counter:

 for i, stop in enumerate(trail_stops):
 print(f"{i}: {stop}")

Looping over two lists together? `zip()` pairs them up:

 for name, distance in zip(names, distances):
 print(f"{name}: {distance} km")

A generator is a function that produces values one at a time, on demand, using `yield` instead of `return` — useful when a sequence is large or even infinite, since it never builds the whole thing in memory at once:

 def countdown(n):
 while n > 0:
 yield n
 n -= 1

A generator expression is the lazy cousin of a list comprehension — swap the square brackets for parentheses: `sum(n**2 for n in range(1000000))` never builds the full list of squares in memory, just streams and sums them one at a time.

The `itertools` module has building blocks for chaining, combining, and slicing iterators efficiently once you outgrow simple loops — worth a skim once these fundamentals feel automatic.

— Based on: Python Tricks 6.1–6.7

lessons.title: Dictionary Tricks
lessons.summary: Defaults, sorting, and merging — the moves you'll reach for constantly.
lessons.body:
A handful of dictionary patterns come up so often they're worth knowing by heart.

`.get(key, default)` avoids a crash when a key might not exist:

 pace = hiker.get("pace", "unknown")

`collections.defaultdict` goes a step further — it auto-creates a default value the first time a new key is used, which is perfect for counting or grouping:

 from collections import defaultdict
 counts = defaultdict(int)
 for word in words:
 counts[word] += 1

Sorting a dictionary by its values (not its keys) is common when ranking something — most-visited trail, highest score:

 sorted(hiker_visits.items(), key=lambda pair: pair[1], reverse=True)

A dictionary can stand in for a switch/case statement, which Python doesn't have natively — mapping a condition directly to a function or value is often cleaner than a long if/elif chain:

 action = {"north": go_north, "south": go_south}.get(direction, go_nowhere)

Merging two dictionaries is a one-liner in modern Python: `combined = dict_a | dict_b` (the second dictionary's values win on any overlapping keys). And for genuinely readable debug output of a nested dictionary, `pprint.pprint()` beats a plain `print()` every time.

— Based on: Python Tricks 7.1–7.6

lessons.title: Pattern Matching with Regular Expressions
lessons.summary: Finding and extracting text patterns with regex.
lessons.body:
A regular expression (regex) is a mini-language for describing patterns in text. Python's `re` module compiles a pattern into a reusable object:

 import re
 phone_pattern = re.compile(r"\d{3}-\d{3}-\d{4}")
 match = phone_pattern.search("Call me at 555-123-4567")
 if match:
 print(match.group())

`\d` means "a digit," `{3}` means "exactly three of the previous thing," and parentheses create groups you can extract separately. `?` makes the previous item optional, `*` means "zero or more," and `+` means "one or more."

`findall()` returns every match in a string as a list, which is often more useful than a single `search()`:

 emails = re.findall(r"[\w.+-]+@[\w-]+\.[\w.-]+", text)

`sub()` finds and replaces: `re.sub(r"\s+", " ", messy_text)` collapses any run of whitespace down to a single space — a genuinely common cleanup step.

Regex patterns get unreadable fast once they're complex. The `re.VERBOSE` flag lets you spread a pattern across multiple lines with comments explaining each piece — worth using the moment a pattern stops being obvious at a glance.

— Based on: Automate the Boring Stuff ch.7

lessons.title: Organizing Files
lessons.summary: Copying, moving, and archiving files programmatically.
lessons.body:
The `shutil` module handles the operations a file manager does with drag-and-drop: `shutil.copy(src, dst)` copies a file, `shutil.move(src, dst)` moves or renames it, and `shutil.rmtree(folder)` deletes an entire folder tree — carefully, since that last one is permanent.

For safer deletion during development, the `send2trash` module sends files to the system trash instead of deleting them outright, so mistakes are recoverable.

Walking a whole directory tree — visiting every file in every subfolder — is a common task:

 import os
 for folder, subfolders, files in os.walk("photos"):
 for filename in files:
 print(os.path.join(folder, filename))

The `zipfile` module reads and creates ZIP archives without any external tools:

 import zipfile
 with zipfile.ZipFile("backup.zip", "w") as zf:
 zf.write("notes.txt")

Combining `os.walk()` with `zipfile.ZipFile` is exactly how you'd script a folder backup — walk every file, add each one to the archive, done. This kind of small, boring automation is where Python starts paying for itself in real time saved.

— Based on: Automate the Boring Stuff ch.9

lessons.title: CSV Files and JSON Data
lessons.summary: Reading, writing, and reshaping structured data.
lessons.body:
CSV (comma-separated values) is the most common plain-text format for tabular data, and Python's `csv` module handles the fiddly quoting rules for you:

 import csv
 with open("hikes.csv") as f:
 reader = csv.reader(f)
 for row in reader:
 print(row)

`csv.DictReader` is often more convenient — it reads each row as a dictionary keyed by the header row, so you access columns by name instead of by position.

JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is the standard format for structured data exchanged over the web, and it maps almost directly onto Python's own dictionaries and lists:

 import json
 with open("hikes.json") as f:
 data = json.load(f)
 print(json.dumps(data, indent=2)) # pretty-printed

`json.loads()`/`json.dumps()` work on strings directly (useful for API responses), while `json.load()`/`json.dump()` work on open file objects.

A common real task is reshaping data between the two: read a folder of CSVs, combine them, and write out one clean JSON summary — exactly the kind of task that used to take an afternoon by hand and takes a few lines of Python instead.

— Based on: Automate the Boring Stuff ch.14

lessons.title: Time, Scheduling, and Subprocess
lessons.summary: Working with dates, delays, and running other programs.
lessons.body:
The `time` module gives you the basics: `time.time()` returns the current moment as a number of seconds since a fixed reference point, and `time.sleep(5)` pauses execution for 5 seconds — useful for pacing a loop that shouldn't run flat-out.

The `datetime` module is richer, giving you calendar-aware objects:

 import datetime
 now = datetime.datetime.now()
 print(now.strftime("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M"))

`datetime` objects support arithmetic too — subtracting one from another gives you a `timedelta` representing the difference, handy for "how many days until the trip."

For running something on a recurring schedule without relying on the operating system's own scheduler, the third-party `schedule` module offers a readable API: `schedule.every().day.at("09:00").do(send_reminder)`.

The `subprocess` module lets a Python script launch and control other programs on the system — running a shell command and capturing its output, for example. It's the modern, safer replacement for the older `os.system()`, and it's how Python scripts glue themselves into a larger toolchain of existing command-line tools.

— Based on: Automate the Boring Stuff ch.15

lessons.title: Email and Text Notifications
lessons.summary: Sending programmatic alerts from a script.
lessons.body:
Python's built-in `smtplib` module can send email through any SMTP server (like Gmail's), which is how a script can notify you when something finishes or needs attention:

 import smtplib
 server = smtplib.SMTP_SSL("smtp.gmail.com", 465)
 server.login("you@gmail.com", "app_password")
 server.sendmail("you@gmail.com", "you@gmail.com", "Subject: Done\n\nTrail backup complete.")
 server.quit()

Note the "app password" — most modern email providers require a special generated password for scripts rather than your real login, since that's more secure and easier to revoke later without changing your main password.

For *reading* email programmatically (checking an inbox rather than sending), the third-party `imapclient` module is a common choice, working over the IMAP protocol.

For SMS text notifications, there's no free built-in option — you'd sign up with a texting API service (Twilio is the most common) and call its API with `requests`, which you'll cover properly in the Working with APIs lesson.

The practical pattern this all supports: a long-running script (a backup job, a scraper, a scheduled task) sends itself an email or text the moment it finishes or fails, so you don't have to babysit it.

— Based on: Automate the Boring Stuff ch.16

lessons.title: Manipulating Images
lessons.summary: Cropping, resizing, and batch-editing photos with Pillow.
lessons.body:
The third-party Pillow library (`pip install Pillow`, imported as `PIL`) is the standard tool for working with images in Python:

 from PIL import Image
 img = Image.open("photo.jpg")
 print(img.size) # (width, height)
 resized = img.resize((800, 600))
 resized.save("photo_small.jpg")

Cropping takes a box of coordinates: `img.crop((left, top, right, bottom))`. Rotating and flipping are one-liners too: `img.rotate(90)`, `img.transpose(Image.FLIP_LEFT_RIGHT)`.

Pasting one image onto another — for a watermark, say — combines `Image.open()` for both images with `.paste(watermark, (x, y))`.

For drawing directly onto an image (text, shapes, annotations), Pillow's `ImageDraw` module gives you a simple canvas API:

 from PIL import ImageDraw
 draw = ImageDraw.Draw(img)
 draw.text((10, 10), "Sendero", fill="white")

The genuinely useful automation here is almost always batch processing — looping over every file in a folder with `os.listdir()` and applying the same resize, watermark, or format conversion to each one, turning a tedious manual task into a script that runs in seconds.

— Based on: Automate the Boring Stuff ch.17

lessons.title: Controlling the Keyboard and Mouse
lessons.summary: GUI automation for repetitive on-screen tasks.
lessons.body:
The third-party `pyautogui` module can move the mouse, click, type, and take screenshots — effectively controlling the computer the way a human would, which makes it useful for automating repetitive tasks in programs that don't offer their own automation API.

 import pyautogui
 pyautogui.moveTo(100, 200)
 pyautogui.click()
 pyautogui.typewrite("Hello!", interval=0.05)

Because this controls the *actual* mouse and keyboard, `pyautogui` includes a built-in fail-safe: quickly moving the mouse to a screen corner aborts the script immediately — an essential safety net while a script is still being tested, since a runaway automation loop can otherwise be hard to interrupt.

`pyautogui.screenshot()` captures the screen, and `pyautogui.locateOnScreen("button.png")` can find a specific image on screen and return its location — useful for clicking a button that moves around or isn't always in a fixed spot.

This kind of automation is genuinely powerful but also the most fragile category covered so far — it depends on exact screen positions and resolutions, so it tends to break the moment a window is resized or moved. Reach for it only when a program truly offers no better way (no API, no command-line option) to automate the task.

— Based on: Automate the Boring Stuff ch.18

lessons.title: Web Scraping
lessons.summary: Pulling structured data out of web pages.
lessons.body:
The `requests` library is the standard way to fetch a web page's content:

 import requests
 response = requests.get("https://example.com")
 response.raise_for_status() # throws an error if the request failed
 html = response.text

Raw HTML is messy to search manually, which is where BeautifulSoup comes in — it parses HTML into a navigable structure you can query with CSS-style selectors:

 from bs4 import BeautifulSoup
 soup = BeautifulSoup(html, "html.parser")
 headlines = soup.select("h2.headline")
 for h in headlines:
 print(h.get_text())

`.select()` takes a CSS selector (the same syntax used in stylesheets — `.classname`, `#id`, `tag`) and returns every matching element. `.get_text()` strips out the HTML tags and leaves just the readable text; `["href"]`-style access pulls a specific attribute off a tag, like a link's URL.

Some pages load their real content with JavaScript after the initial page loads, which `requests` alone can't see — that's when the `selenium` module comes in, since it drives an actual browser and can wait for dynamic content to appear before reading the page.

Always check a site's terms of service and `robots.txt` before scraping it at any real scale, and add a small delay between requests so you're not hammering someone else's server.

— Based on: Automate the Boring Stuff ch.11

lessons.title: Working with Excel Spreadsheets
lessons.summary: Reading, editing, and formatting .xlsx files programmatically.
lessons.body:
The `openpyxl` module reads and writes Excel's .xlsx format directly:

 import openpyxl
 wb = openpyxl.load_workbook("hikes.xlsx")
 sheet = wb.active
 print(sheet["A1"].value)
 for row in sheet.iter_rows(min_row=2, values_only=True):
 print(row)

A workbook contains one or more sheets, each made of cells addressed either by name ("B3") or by row/column number. Writing works the same way in reverse: `sheet["A1"] = "Trail Name"`, then `wb.save("hikes.xlsx")`.

A very common real task is checking every row against some rule and fixing the ones that don't match — for example, scanning a price column and correcting any value below a minimum. Looping through rows with `iter_rows()` and writing corrections back is exactly that pattern.

Beyond raw values, `openpyxl` can also touch formatting: font objects control bold/italic/size/color, `sheet.merge_cells("A1:C1")` merges a header across columns, and `sheet.freeze_panes = "A2"` keeps a header row visible while scrolling. It can even generate charts from the data already in the sheet — genuinely useful for turning a script's output straight into a report someone can open in Excel.

— Based on: Automate the Boring Stuff ch.12

lessons.title: Working with PDF and Word Documents
lessons.summary: Extracting and generating text from common document formats.
lessons.body:
PDFs are notoriously inconsistent to extract text from since the format was designed for *appearance*, not structure — but for straightforward PDFs, a library like `pypdf` gets you most of the way:

 from pypdf import PdfReader
 reader = PdfReader("guide.pdf")
 for page in reader.pages:
 print(page.extract_text())

Combining PDFs is a common task: create a `PdfWriter`, add pages from multiple source PDFs, and save the result as one file — a script can do in seconds what used to mean opening several files by hand.

For Word documents (.docx), the `python-docx` module reads and writes them directly:

 from docx import Document
 doc = Document()
 doc.add_heading("Trail Notes", level=1)
 doc.add_paragraph("Started at dawn, cool and clear.")
 doc.save("notes.docx")

Reading an existing .docx works the same way in reverse — `Document("notes.docx").paragraphs` gives you each paragraph's text and style, so you can search or reformat an existing document programmatically rather than by hand.

Both of these libraries turn "I need to generate/edit fifty similar documents" from an afternoon of copy-paste into a script that runs once.

— Based on: Automate the Boring Stuff ch.13

lessons.title: Generating and Downloading Data
lessons.summary: Visualizing data and pulling real datasets into a program.
lessons.body:
The `matplotlib` library is the standard for basic charts in Python:

 import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
 plt.plot([1, 2, 3], [10, 20, 15])
 plt.xlabel("Day")
 plt.ylabel("Distance (km)")
 plt.savefig("chart.png")

For anything more visually polished or interactive, `plotly` produces charts you can zoom and hover over, and exports cleanly to a web page.

Real datasets almost always arrive as CSV or JSON — a weather archive, an earthquake feed, a government dataset. Once downloaded (often with `requests`, covered earlier), the pattern is consistent: load it (`csv` or `json` module), pull out the fields you care about, and hand those lists of numbers to `matplotlib` or `plotly`.

A useful habit when working with a new dataset: print the first few rows and inspect the column names before writing any real processing code — real-world data is messy (missing values, inconsistent formatting, unexpected types), and understanding its actual shape upfront saves a lot of debugging later.

This lesson is the bridge between "I know how to read a file" and "I can turn a raw dataset into a chart that tells a story" — genuinely one of the most immediately rewarding things Python is good at.

— Based on: Python Crash Course ch.15–16

lessons.title: Working with APIs
lessons.summary: Calling web services and working with their JSON responses.
lessons.body:
An API (Application Programming Interface) lets a program request data from a web service directly, instead of scraping a web page meant for humans. Most modern APIs speak JSON:

 import requests
 response = requests.get("https://api.example.com/trails", params={"region": "PR"})
 data = response.json()
 for trail in data["results"]:
 print(trail["name"], trail["distance_km"])

`response.json()` parses the response body straight into Python dictionaries and lists — no manual parsing needed, since `requests` handles it.

Many APIs require an API key — a personal token identifying who's making the request, usually sent as a header or a query parameter — both to track usage and to enforce rate limits (how many requests you're allowed per minute or day). Respecting a documented rate limit isn't optional; exceeding it typically gets your key temporarily blocked.

Combining an API call with `matplotlib` from the previous lesson is a natural next step: pull live data (weather, prices, statistics), then chart it immediately — the same skill that powers dashboards and live-data apps, just at a smaller, personal scale.

Reading API documentation carefully is a real skill in itself — the exact URL structure, required parameters, and response shape vary completely from one API to the next, and there's no substitute for reading the specific docs for whatever service you're calling.

— Based on: Python Crash Course ch.17

lessons.title: Capstone Option A — Arcade Game
lessons.summary: Applying everything so far to build a small game with pygame.
lessons.body:
This capstone builds a simple arcade-style game (a ship that fires at descending aliens) using the third-party `pygame` library, and it's a genuinely good test of everything covered so far — classes for the ship and aliens, lists to track active bullets and enemies, loops for the game's main cycle, and functions to keep the logic organized.

The core shape of almost any pygame project is the same:

 import pygame
 pygame.init()
 screen = pygame.display.set_mode((800, 600))
 running = True
 while running:
 for event in pygame.event.get():
 if event.type == pygame.QUIT:
 running = False
 # update game state, then draw everything
 pygame.display.flip()

That `while running` loop — check input, update state, redraw, repeat — is the "game loop," and it runs dozens of times per second for the entire life of the program.

Collision detection (did a bullet hit an alien?) usually comes from pygame's built-in `Rect` objects and their `.colliderect()` method rather than manual coordinate math. Scoring and levels are just variables that update in response to those collisions.

As a real exercise: build the base game, then extend it with one original feature — a power-up, a second enemy type, a high-score file saved with `json`.

— Based on: Python Crash Course ch.12–14

lessons.title: Capstone Option B — Web App with Django
lessons.summary: Building and deploying a small web application.
lessons.body:
Django is a full-featured web framework — it handles URL routing, database models, an admin interface, and page templates, so you're writing your app's actual logic rather than reinventing web-server plumbing.

A Django project is organized into "apps" (a project can contain several) with a consistent structure: `models.py` defines your data (each Python class becomes a database table), `views.py` defines what happens when a URL is requested, and `templates/` holds the HTML.

 # models.py
 from django.db import models
 class LogEntry(models.Model):
 trail_name = models.CharField(max_length=100)
 date = models.DateField()
 notes = models.TextField()

After defining a model, `python manage.py makemigrations` and `python manage.py migrate` create the actual database table for it — Django writes the SQL for you.

Django also ships with a built-in user account system (registration, login, permissions) rather than making you build authentication from scratch, and styling a project with a framework like Bootstrap gets a reasonable-looking interface without needing deep CSS knowledge.

A realistic capstone here: a small personal log app — trail hikes, books read, workouts — with a form to add entries and a page listing them, deployed so it's reachable from a phone as well as a laptop.

— Based on: Python Crash Course ch.18–20

lessons.title: Pythonic Productivity Techniques
lessons.summary: Exploring modules, isolating dependencies, and a peek under the hood.
lessons.body:
A few habits make working in Python day-to-day noticeably smoother.

`dir(obj)` lists every attribute and method an object has, and `help(obj)` prints its documentation — both work on anything, including modules you've just imported, and are genuinely faster than searching online for "what methods does a Python list have."

As a project grows and starts depending on third-party libraries (Pillow, requests, pygame, and so on), a virtual environment keeps those dependencies isolated per-project instead of polluting the whole system's Python install:

 python3 -m venv myproject_env
 source myproject_env/bin/activate
 pip install requests

Once activated, `pip install` only affects that environment — switching projects means switching environments, and each one can have a completely different, non-conflicting set of installed packages.

Under the hood, Python compiles your source code into bytecode (a lower-level intermediate form, stored in `__pycache__` as .pyc files) before actually running it — you don't need to manage this yourself, but knowing it exists explains why a program's first run after an edit is sometimes marginally slower than the next one.

None of this changes what your code does — it's entirely about the workflow around writing it, and it's the kind of thing that starts mattering once a personal script becomes an actual maintained project.

— Based on: Python Tricks 8.1–8.3
